title: availability-sla-storyboard-and-competitive-notes
summary: Working storyboard for how Redwood presents availability guarantees and graceful degradation to customers and prospects. Includes proposed SLA language, short incident narratives at multiple severity tiers, micro-scripts for sales and CS, and a concise competitor comparison focusing on runbook choices and customer impact.
audience: Sales SEs, Solutions Engineering, Growth PMs, GTM leadership
positioning_notes: Goal: make availability a seller enablement story, not just a legal checkbox. Emphasize deterministic behavior during constrained capacity: predictable trade-offs (latency vs quality), transparent observability, and automated fallback controls that keep critical user journeys online. Avoid defensive language; lead with 'we plan for continuity' and 'we give customers operational controls'.
competitor_comparison:
Snapshot vs three typical market approaches:
- Provider A (managed endpoints): often offers cross-region failover but treats it as coarse (DNS-level) and customers see a hard switch with cold caches and high latency. No model-variant fallback.
- Provider B (simple autoscale): relies on broad autoscaling and burst credits; when exhausted, requests queue or are rate-limited. Customers face opaque throttling and retried requests.
- Provider C (self-hosted runtime vendors): provide deep control but require customer ops to implement fallback layers; less polished observability and rollout tooling.
Redwood differences to highlight in sales conversations: model-variant fallbacks (degrade to a compatible quantized/shorter-context variant with explicit quality delta), prefix/KV cache preservation across failovers, per-route SLOs that can be tuned by customers, and clear post-incident artifacts (trace links, token-level cost/latency breakdowns) so customers can correlate business impact to technical signals.
customer_scripts:
Two short scripts for customer-facing teams:
1) 'Partial-impairment' email (for transient regional congestion):
  Subject: Brief service note: routing to alternate capacity to preserve your user flows
  Body: We're proactively routing some traffic to alternate capacity to keep your most critical calls (auth, payments, chat) within latency targets. You may notice slightly different model latency for long context requests; this is intentional to preserve throughput. No action required — this preserves availability while we scale capacity.
2) Sales quick line for objections about degradation:
  Prospect: 'What happens if your primary region goes down?'
  SE: 'We detect capacity constraints automatically, route by policy (latency-first or cost-first), and can fall back to a compatible model variant in another region while preserving cached prefixes. That means the product stays responsive for core flows and your SLAs remain measurable — not a blind failover.'
incident_playbook_steps:
Condensed public-friendly incident narratives (3 severity tiers) to use in status updates or one-pagers:
- SEV2 (degrading latency in region): immediate actions: shift routing to secondary region for non-sensitive traffic, enable short-context model variant for long-running streams, notify customers affected via routing tag list. Narrative: 'We observed increased queuing for long-context generation in eu-west-1. To maintain responsiveness for critical flows we routed non-sensitive traffic to nearby capacity and temporarily served long contexts on a shorter-context variant; customer impact limited to a small increase in variance for multi-turn sessions.'
- SEV1 (partial capacity outage): immediate actions: enable canary fallbacks per-customer, raise runbook to SRE and account teams, open dedicated Slack channel with impacted customers. Narrative: 'A capacity degradation affected a subset of dedicated pools; we activated pre-configured canary fallbacks and prioritized customer-pinned routes. Most customers remained within their latency targets; a small number experienced elevated error rates for heavy batch workloads while we rebalanced GPUs.'
- SEV0 (complete region outage): immediate actions: engage cross-region DR play, replace with warmed standby clusters, execute customer-facing SLA incident with timeline and compensation options. Narrative: 'We experienced a full outage in region X affecting hosted inference. We failed over to warm capacity in region Y and served model-variant fallbacks while restoring stateful caches. We are issuing an incident report with timelines, root cause, and any crediting per contractual SLA.'
measurement_and_signals: Key signals we promise to instrument and share: per-route p95/p99 latency, token rate and cost broken down by model variant, cache hit ratio (prefix and KV), cross-region failover counts, model-variant switch events per-customer, and error-rate delta by endpoint. Suggested SLA language: 'We target 99.5% availability for production routes measured over monthly windows, with clearly documented fallback behaviors that may alter latency/quality but preserve connectivity. Detailed per-route telemetry will be provided during incidents.'
objection_handling:
Short counters for common sales objections:
- 'Degradation is risky' -> 'We codify degradation: deterministic fallbacks with measured quality deltas and opt-in policies per-route.'
- 'You can't be transparent about outages' -> 'We expose traceable artifacts (trace links, model-variant logs, token-level cost/latency) so customers can verify impact.'
- 'Cross-region failover causes cold caches' -> 'We maintain warmed standby capacity for critical customers and preserve prefix caches where possible; fallbacks prioritize cache-preserving routes.'
